I keep asking how anyone carries this. I want to know what the steady ones know.
Everyone I love will leave or I will leave them. I cannot stop thinking about it since Dad died.

key_verses.sanskrit: यथा काष्ठं च काष्ठं च समेयातां महोदधौ / समेत्य च व्यपेयातां तद्वद्भूतसमागमः
key_verses.gist: As two logs meet on the ocean and drift apart, so do living beings meet.

key_verses.sanskrit: सुखात्त्वं दुःखमापन्नः पुनरापत्स्यसे सुखम् / न नित्यं लभते दुःखं न नित्यं लभते सुखम्
key_verses.gist: From happiness you fell into sorrow; you will come to happiness again. No one keeps sorrow forever.

content_hook: Two pieces of driftwood meet on the ocean. A grieving king was asked to think about what happens next.

title: Pingala waits all night for someone who does not come, and then stops
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 173, verses 58 to 64 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ), told to Senajit
the_moment: Pingala, a courtesan, has dressed and waited at the meeting place for the man she loves. He does not come. The night wears on and she is left alone with it.
what_they_did: In that hard hour she sets her mind on calm instead of on the door. She says: I was mad, waiting so long for one who was not mad for me, while the true beloved was always near me and I never went to him. No one will deceive me again in the shape of love. I am awake now.
the_turn: 'The one who has no hope sleeps in peace; to be without that hope is the highest happiness. Turning hope into no-hope, Pingala sleeps peacefully' (12.173.64).
outcome: She sleeps. The friend uses her song to steady a grieving king, and the tradition repeats her line for centuries.
whole_arc_note: Her 'nairashya' is giving up the hope that hangs on another person's coming, not giving up on life. Read it as freedom from waiting, never as despair. Her trade is not the point; she is the teacher here.
teaching: Expectation that hangs on someone else keeps you awake; letting it go is what lets you sleep.
modern_parallels: I sat up till 2 am waiting for his message. It never came. I am tired of being that person.
I keep refreshing my email for the offer letter and it is ruining my evenings.
She said she would call after the wedding. I have stopped checking my phone, and I slept for the first time in weeks.
I have waited three years for my father to say he is proud of me.

key_verses.sanskrit: सुखं निराशः स्वपिति नैराश्यं परमं सुखम् / आशामनाशां कृत्वा हि सुखं स्वपिति पिङ्गला
key_verses.gist: The one without expectation sleeps in peace; turning hope into no-hope, Pingala sleeps.

key_verses.sanskrit: उन्मत्ताऽहमनुन्मत्तं कान्तमन्ववसं चिरम् / अन्तिके रमणं सन्तं नैनमध्यगमं पुरा
key_verses.gist: Mad, I waited long on one who was not mad for me, and never went to the beloved who was always near.

content_hook: She waited all night for him. Then she said one sentence and went to sleep.

title: Mithila is on fire, and the king says nothing of his is burning
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 223, verses 1 to 18 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); the verse also quoted at 12.17.19 and 12.176.56
the_moment: Janaka is tested. His city of Mithila is set ablaze in front of him and the people crowd round to see what their king will do as everything he owns goes up in flames.
what_they_did: He does not tremble (12.223.16). Asked by the people, he says: my wealth is endless, for nothing is mine. With Mithila burning, nothing of mine burns.
the_turn: The line itself: 'anantam bata me vittam yasya me nasti kinchana; mithilayam pradiptayam na me kinchana dahyate' (12.223.17). Hearing the words that came from his heart, the tester restored the city (12.223.18).
outcome: The city stands again. Yudhishthira and Bhishma both quote the verse later as the mark of a free person who still rules.
whole_arc_note: Janaka did not abandon Mithila; he went on ruling it well. The verse describes a ruler who acts fully and owns nothing inside. Do not use it to tell someone their house or savings should not matter to them; use it for the fear of losing what you hold.
teaching: One who holds nothing as 'mine' loses nothing when it burns, and so can act without fear.
modern_parallels: The market crashed and took half my savings. I want to know how to stay the same person through it.
The fire alarm went off in our building and I realised I was more afraid for my laptop than anything.
I run a company and I lie awake afraid of losing it. I want to run it like it is not my identity.
Our startup is on fire every week. I need a way to work in the middle of it without burning with it.

key_verses.sanskrit: अनन्तं वत मे वित्तं भाव्यं मे नास्ति किंचन / मिथिलायां प्रदीप्तायां न मे किंचन दह्यते
key_verses.gist: My wealth is endless, for nothing is mine. With Mithila burning, nothing of mine burns.

key_verses.sanskrit: अनन्तमिव मे वित्तं यस्य मे नास्ति किंचन / मिथिलायां प्रदीप्तायां न मे दह्यति किंचन
key_verses.gist: The same verse as quoted after Manki's song.

content_hook: His whole city was burning in front of him. The king said: nothing of mine is on fire.

title: Manki puts his last money into two young bulls, and a camel runs off with them
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 176, verses 4 to 54 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Manki has tried again and again to make money and failed each time. With the little he has left he buys a pair of young bulls to train. Yoked together, they bolt at a sitting camel, which rises with them hanging from its neck and runs off. He watches his last investment dangle like a pair of jewels from the camel's neck, dying.
dilemma: Try once more for wealth, or ask what all this wanting is doing to him.
what_they_did: First he blames fate: however skilled and earnest, no one gets wealth that is not ordained (12.176.9-12). Then, out of that weariness, he turns on desire itself and speaks to it directly.
the_turn: 'Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all' (12.176.25). All the pleasures of this world and the next are not worth a sixteenth of the happiness of craving's end (12.176.51).
outcome: Bhishma says that through the loss of his bulls Manki reached the deathless; he cut the root of desire (12.176.54).
whole_arc_note: The arc moves from 'it is all fate' to 'it is my craving'. Do not stop at the fatalist lines in the middle. Also, this is not advice to stop working; Bhishma tells it to a king asking how a man who fails to gain wealth can still be happy.
teaching: Craving is born of one's own imagining; stop feeding it and it dies at the root.
modern_parallels: My third business failed. I put my last savings into it and watched it go.
I lost money on a stock everyone said was safe, and I realised I had been gambling for a feeling, not a future.
Every time I almost make it something absurd happens. I am done blaming luck.
I keep chasing the next raise and the wanting never goes away.

key_verses.gist: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my imagining. I will not imagine you, and you will be gone.

key_verses.sanskrit: यच्च कामसुखं लोके यच्च दिव्यं महत्सुखम् / तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्यैते नार्हतः षोडशीं कलाम्
key_verses.gist: No pleasure here or in heaven is worth a sixteenth of the happiness of craving's end.

key_verses.sanskrit: दम्यनाशकृते मङ्किरमृतत्वं किलागमत् / अच्छिनत्काममूलं स तेन प्राप परां गतिम्
key_verses.gist: Through the loss of his bulls Manki reached the deathless; he cut the root of desire.

content_hook: He spent his last money on two bulls. A camel stood up and ran away with them.

title: A son tells his father not to wait for later
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 174 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: A learned man lives by the plan: study first, then household, then sacrifices, then the forest when old. His son Medhavin asks what a wise person should do when life is running out so fast. The father recites the plan. The son says: the world is under attack and surrounded, and the days that cannot be stopped are falling; why do you speak as if you had time?
what_they_did: The father, startled, asks what he means. The son answers: the world is struck by death and hemmed in by old age; the days and nights fall one after another and do not return (12.174.9). What is due tomorrow, do today; what is due in the afternoon, do in the morning; death does not wait to see whether your work is done (12.174.15).
the_turn: 'What will wealth or relatives or a wife do for you, who will die? Look for the self hidden in the cave of the heart. Where have your grandfathers gone, and your father?' (12.174.38).
outcome: The father did as his son told him (12.174.39). Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to do the same.
whole_arc_note: The child is the teacher and the parent listens; keep that. The urgency is about the inner work, not about cramming more tasks into a day.
teaching: Death does not wait for the work to be done; do the work that matters now, not after.
framework: Medhavin's order: 1. Stop speaking of 'later' as if it were promised. 2. Bring tomorrow's essential thing into today. 3. Ask what will still be yours at the end, and turn toward that.
modern_parallels: I keep telling myself I will start meditating once the kids are settled. My daughter asked me when that would be.
I am 52 and I have been saying 'after retirement' for twenty years.
My son asked why I never do the things I keep saying I love. I had no answer.
I want to call my father and fix things but I keep waiting for the right time.

key_verses.sanskrit: श्वः कार्यमद्य कुर्वीत पूर्वाह्णे चापराह्णिकम् / नहि प्रतीक्षते मृत्युः कृतमस्य न वा कृतम्
key_verses.gist: Do tomorrow's work today and the afternoon's in the morning; death does not wait.

key_verses.sanskrit: किं ते धनैर्बान्धवैर्वापि किं ते / किं ते दारैर्ब्राह्मण यो मरिष्यसि / आत्मानमन्विच्छ गुहां प्रविष्टं / पितामहास्ते क्व गताः पिता च
key_verses.gist: What will wealth or kin do for you who will die? Seek the self in the cave of the heart.

content_hook: A father explained his life plan. His son asked: and what if you do not get to 'later'?

title: Knocked down by a rich man's chariot, Kashyapa decides to die, and a jackal talks to him about hands
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyaya 178 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: A proud, wealthy merchant drives his chariot into the young ascetic Kashyapa and knocks him down. Hurt, humiliated and angry, Kashyapa lies there and says: I will die; a poor man has no reason to live (12.178.5-6). He lies silent, waiting for death.
what_they_did: A jackal (Indra in disguise) sits by him and talks. Every creature wants a human birth, he says, and you have one; you should not die over a slight. Then he speaks about hands: we long for hands the way you long for money; there is no gain greater than hands (12.178.12). Without them I cannot pull out a thorn or brush off the insects that bite me (12.178.13, 20).
the_turn: The jackal shows him what he already has before anything he lacks. He also admits his own past: he was a learned man who mocked and argued, and was born a jackal for it.
outcome: Kashyapa recognises the speaker as Indra, honours him and goes home. The chapter is Bhishma's answer to 'what does a person stand on: kin, work, wealth or wisdom?' and its answer is wisdom.
whole_arc_note: This is a story about wanting to die after humiliation and money envy. It must be served only where there is no risk, and the jackal's turn is gratitude for what one has, never 'others have it worse, so stop'. Keep the merchant's arrogance in view; Kashyapa was wronged.
teaching: Before counting what you lack, count what you have; a human life with hands is already the great gain.
modern_parallels: A man in a BMW cut me off and screamed at me and I went home feeling worthless for days.
My cousin flaunts his money every family dinner and I leave thinking my life is pointless.
I got humiliated in front of the team and that night I thought I would be better off gone.
I keep comparing my salary to my school friends and I forget I can walk, think and work.

key_verses.sanskrit: पाणिमद्भ्यः स्पृहाऽस्माकं यथा तव धनस्य वै / न पाणिलाभादधिको लाभः कश्चन विद्यते
key_verses.gist: We long for hands as you long for money; there is no gain greater than having hands.

key_verses.sanskrit: आर्तः स पतितः क्रुद्धस्त्यक्त्वाऽऽत्मानमथाब्रवीत् / मरिष्याम्यधनस्येह जीवितार्थो न विद्यते
key_verses.gist: Hurt, fallen and angry, giving up on himself, he said: I will die; a poor man has no reason to live.

content_hook: A rich man's chariot knocked him into the dirt. A jackal came and asked him to look at his hands.

title: The king who lost everything, asked by the winner how it feels
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyayas 230 to 231 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Bali was the most generous and powerful king of the asuras. Now he has lost his kingdom and lives hidden in a deserted house in the shape of a donkey. Indra, the victor, comes looking for him and taunts him: how do you feel now, stripped of everything?
what_they_did: Bali answers without self-pity and without flattering the winner. It does not suit you, he says, to boast over one who has lost what you now have (12.230.31). He explains why he does not grieve: he has seen that his rise and fall are turns of time, and everything here has an end (12.231.7).
the_turn: 'Time takes everything; time gives everything. Do not make a boast of your own strength, Shakra' (12.231.27). And the fortune you think lives with you has lived with thousands of Indras before you and has stayed with none (12.231.62).
outcome: Indra leaves chastened. Bhishma tells it to answer how a king who has lost his throne should walk the earth.
whole_arc_note: Bali's calm is not resignation; he keeps his dignity and corrects the winner to his face. Use for loss of status, never to tell a wronged person their loss does not matter.
teaching: Fortune moves on by time's turn; the one who knows this neither crumbles in a fall nor gloats in a rise.
modern_parallels: I was CEO for nine years and got pushed out. My successor called to ask how I was 'coping'.
After the layoff a former colleague who stayed kept checking in a little too sweetly.
Our family business went under and the relatives who used to ask for favours now ask how we manage.
I was the top performer for years. Now I am not, and people are watching how I take it.

key_verses.gist: The fortune you think rests with you has lived with thousands of Indras before you and stayed with none.

key_verses.sanskrit: कालः सर्वं समादत्ते कालः सर्वं प्रयच्छति / कालेन विहितं सर्वं मा कृथाः शक्र पौरुषम्
key_verses.gist: Time takes everything, time gives everything; do not boast of your own strength.
It does not suit you, who have everything, to gloat over me, who have lost it.

content_hook: The winner came to mock the fallen king. The fallen king answered him in one sentence about time.

title: Starving in a famine, the great sage steals dog's meat from an outcaste's hut
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyaya 141 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: A twelve-year drought has emptied the land. Vishvamitra, a great sage, wanders starving. He has found no food for a long time and sees no way to stay alive (12.141.62). At night he creeps into a chandala's hut to steal the haunch of a dog hanging there, and the owner wakes.
dilemma: Keep his purity and die, or eat what his own code forbids and live.
what_they_did: The chandala argues with him: this is not food for you, go beg elsewhere, eating it will not even give you long life (12.141.68). Vishvamitra answers point by point: in a famine there is no other meat, I have no money, I am without hope (12.141.69). One should stay alive by whatever means; living is better than dying, for the living can still do dharma (12.141.65).
the_turn: He takes the meat, but even then he resolves to eat it according to rite, offering first to the gods (12.141.96). He keeps the form of his duty inside the emergency.
outcome: Bhishma says that the rains returned. He tells this to teach that in apad, extreme distress, a wise person keeps himself alive and returns to normal conduct when the crisis passes (12.141.103).
whole_arc_note: Do not reduce this to 'rules do not matter'. The text frames it strictly as apaddharma: true emergency, no other way, argued in the open, and with the inner rule kept where possible. The chandala is shown as articulate and right on many points; do not make him a prop. Caste language is in the text; tell it without endorsing hierarchy.
teaching: In real extremity, staying alive is itself a duty; the code bends for the crisis and returns after it.
framework: Bhishma's test for an emergency exception: 1. Is it truly extreme, with no other way? 2. Can you defend it openly to the person who objects? 3. Keep whatever part of your principle you still can. 4. Return to the ordinary rule when the crisis ends.
modern_parallels: I swore I would never borrow from my in-laws. Then the hospital bill came.
I am a strict vegetarian and on the trek I had to eat whatever the villagers gave us or go without for three days.
I took a job I had always looked down on because the rent was due and there was nothing else.
I broke a promise to myself to keep my family afloat this year and I keep feeling dirty about it.

key_verses.sanskrit: यथायथैव जीवेद्धि तत्कर्तव्यमहेलया / जीवितं मरणाच्छ्रेयो जीवन्धर्ममवाप्नुयात्
key_verses.gist: One should stay alive by whatever means; life is better than death, for the living can still do dharma.

key_verses.sanskrit: न दुर्भिक्षे सुलभं मांसमन्य / च्छ्वपाकमन्ये न च मेऽस्ति वित्तम / क्षुघार्तश्चाहमगतिर्निराशः / श्वजाघनीं ष़ड्सात्साधु मन्ये
key_verses.gist: In a famine there is no other meat, I have no money, I am starving and without hope.

content_hook: The most famous sage in India, starving, was caught stealing dog's meat. Then the argument began.

title: The ascetic proud of birds nesting in his hair is sent to learn from a shopkeeper
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, adhyayas 267 to 270 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Jajali has practised austerity for years, standing so still that birds nested in his matted hair and raised their young there. Looking out over the earth to the sea, he thinks: there is no one like me (12.267.6). A voice from the sky tells him he is wrong: the merchant Tuladhara of Varanasi is wiser, and even he would not speak like this.
what_they_did: Stung, he goes to Varanasi to see this trader. Tuladhara greets him by name before he speaks, and knows about the birds.
the_turn: The shopkeeper's teaching: dharma is to be a friend to all beings, devoted to their good, in deed, thought and word (12.268.9). He weighs fairly, harms no one, neither praises nor blames, and is the same to clod, stone and gold.
outcome: Jajali, the great ascetic, learns from a man at a weighing scale. Both reach peace.
whole_arc_note: The story does not mock austerity; it targets the pride that grows out of it. Do not turn it into 'ordinary work beats spiritual practice'. The point is that goodwill toward all, practised in ordinary dealing, is the measure.
teaching: One who is a friend to all beings in deed, thought and word knows dharma, whatever his work.
modern_parallels: I have done yoga for twelve years and I caught myself looking down on people who have not.
I am the most qualified person in my team and a junior with no degree handles clients better than me.
I fast every Ekadashi and I noticed I have become judgemental about everyone who does not.
My aunt runs a small grocery and she is calmer and kinder than any spiritual teacher I have met.

key_verses.sanskrit: सर्वेषां यः सुहृन्नित्यं सर्वेषां च हिते रतः / कर्मणा मनसा वाचा स धर्मं वेद जाजले
key_verses.gist: The one who is always a friend to all and devoted to their good, in act, thought and word, knows dharma.

key_verses.sanskrit: न मया सदृशोऽस्तीह लोके स्थावरजङ्गमे / अप्सु वैहायसं गच्छेन्मया योऽन्यः सहेति वै
key_verses.gist: There is no one like me in this world.

content_hook: Birds were nesting in his hair, he had meditated so long. Then he was sent to learn from a shopkeeper.

title: Vyasa runs after his grown son calling 'Son!', and only the echo answers
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, the Shuka narrative, adhyayas 333 to 341, the departure at 341 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Vyasa raised his son Shuka himself, taught him everything, and sent him to Janaka to finish his learning. Now Shuka, fully free, rises from the mountain and leaves for good. Vyasa, the greatest sage of his age, follows him with love, calling 'Son!' (12.341.19).
what_they_did: He reaches the peak and finds it split where his son passed. Shuka, now one with everything, answers only with the sound 'bho', and the whole world, mountains and trees, echoes it back (12.341.24-25). Vyasa sits down on the mountainside thinking only of his son (12.341.28).
the_turn: He sees his son's freedom and his own clinging side by side, and he is glad and ashamed at once (12.341.31). Shiva comes to console the grieving father and gives him a shadow like his son that will never leave him (12.341.33, 38).
outcome: Vyasa turns back with great joy, seeing the shadow (12.341.39). He does not get his boy back; he gets something he can live with.
whole_arc_note: Do not cut it at the echo; the father's mixed joy and shame, and Shiva's gentleness with him, are the heart. The son is not dead; he has gone on to his own life. Do not use as consolation after a child's death.
teaching: A parent can be proud of a child's freedom and still ache at being left; both are true, and grace meets the ache.
modern_parallels: My daughter moved to Canada last month. I am so proud of her and I sit in her room every evening.
My son became a monk. Everyone says it is a blessing. I just want to hear him call me Papa.
I raised him to be independent and now he does not need me. I did my job too well.
When the car turned the corner to the airport I kept waving long after they could see me.

key_verses.sanskrit: तं प्रक्रामन्तमाज्ञाय पिता स्नेहसमन्वितः / उत्तमां गतिमास्थाय पृष्ठतोऽनुससार ह
key_verses.gist: Knowing he was leaving, the father, full of love, followed after him.

key_verses.sanskrit: तां मुक्ततां तु विज्ञाय मुनिः पुत्रस्य वै तदा / सक्ततामात्मनश्चैव प्रीतोऽभूद्बीडितश्च ह
key_verses.gist: Seeing his son's freedom and his own attachment, the sage was glad and ashamed.

key_verses.sanskrit: छायां स्वपुत्रसदृशीं सर्वतोऽनपगां सदा / द्रक्ष्यसे त्वं च लोकेऽस्मिन्मत्प्रसादान्महामुने
key_verses.gist: You will always see a shadow like your son, never leaving you.

content_hook: The greatest sage in India chased his grown son up a mountain, calling his name.

title: Death is created, and the first thing she does is weep
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharma section, adhyayas 262 to 264 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); the same story is told by Vyasa to Yudhishthira in Drona Parva after Abhimanyu's death
the_moment: Brahma, angry that the world is overcrowded, begins to burn it. Shiva pleads for the creatures. To relieve the earth, a woman arises from Brahma's body and is told she will take the lives of all beings. She stands with folded hands and weeps. How can one like me be made for such cruel work, she asks; I fear wrongdoing; let me not take children, the old and the innocent (12.264.2-4).
dilemma: Do the work she was made for, or refuse a task that will cause endless grief.
what_they_did: She refuses, goes away and does severe austerities for ages, begging to be released. Brahma will not release her, but he answers her fear: no blame will fall on her. The tears she shed and held in her hands become the diseases; and desire and anger, not she, will end each life at its time (12.264.30-38).
the_turn: 'Death, the illnesses born of your tears, touch the bodies of all at life's end; therefore do not grieve; see it with understanding' (12.264.39).
outcome: She accepts, takes lives at the proper time, and is without fault. The story is told to show the grieving that death is no one's cruelty and no one's personal enemy.
whole_arc_note: The image is Death weeping and not wanting to do it. Keep that. Do not frame death as punishment. Told after Abhimanyu's death to a guilty, grieving Yudhishthira; it consoles by removing the idea that someone malicious took the person away.
teaching: Death comes at its time to every being and is no one's cruelty; seeing this, grief can loosen.
modern_parallels: I keep thinking someone must be to blame for Mom's cancer. The doctors, God, me.
I am a palliative care nurse and some days I feel like I am the one taking them.
My father died at 61 and it felt like something personal had been done to us.
I am angry at death as if it were a person.

key_verses.sanskrit: बालान्वृद्धान्वयस्थांश्च न हरेयमनागसः / प्राणिनः प्राणिनामीश नमस्तेऽस्तु प्रसीद मे
key_verses.gist: Let me not take children, the old or the young, who have done nothing wrong.

key_verses.sanskrit: मृत्योर्ये ते व्याधयश्चाश्चुपाता / मनुष्याणां युज्यते यैः शरीरम् / सर्वेषां वै प्राणिनां प्राणनान्ते / तस्माच्छोकं मा कृथा बुद्ध्य बुद्ध्या
key_verses.gist: The illnesses born of your tears take every being at life's end; so do not grieve, understand.

content_hook: In the Mahabharata, when Death was created, the first thing she did was cry.

title: A father whose son was killed, and the list of the great who also died
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyayas 28 to 30 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); Krishna retells Narada's words to Yudhishthira
the_moment: King Srinjaya's only son, a boy he had prayed for, has been killed by robbers in the forest. The father is drowning in grief. Narada comes to him.
what_they_did: Narada names sixteen kings, each greater, more generous and more righteous than Srinjaya and his son, and says of each: he too died. You, I and all creatures will die without being freed from joy and sorrow; so why such lament? (12.28.14). He ends each life with the same refrain: if he died, who was better than you and your son, do not grieve.
the_turn: When Srinjaya has heard it all and is quieted, Narada, moved, offers a gift. In this story the son is given back (12.30.21). Krishna tells it all to Yudhishthira to lift him out of his own grief over the war dead.
outcome: Yudhishthira hears it; Krishna has to add his own words before he will move. The list of the great dead is the medicine; the return of the boy is a grace the text gives to this one father.
whole_arc_note: Do not present the revival as something a grieving parent can expect; lead with the sixteen kings, and say plainly that the boy's return is a miracle of this story. Not for a parent recently bereaved of a child as a plan-day story unless the plan is explicitly about reading the text, because the happy ending can wound.
teaching: Even the greatest and most righteous die; no one is singled out, and seeing this lightens the weight.
modern_parallels: Why him? Why my boy? I need to know it is not only us.
After the accident I kept reading about other families who lost children. It was strange comfort.
My grief feels like an injustice done only to me.
Reading obituaries of people far greater than my father somehow helped.

key_verses.gist: You, I and all creatures will die without being freed from joy and sorrow; why then such lament?

key_verses.sanskrit: अहं ते दयितं पुत्रं प्रेतराजवशं गतम् / पुनर्दास्यामि तद्रूपं मा शुचः पृथिवीपते
key_verses.gist: Narada: I will give back your dear son who has gone to the king of the dead; do not grieve.

content_hook: A king lost his only son. The sage answered with sixteen names.

title: The hunter who sheltered under a tree, and the bird who fed him
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, adhyayas 143 to 148 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: A cruel fowler, caught in a freezing storm, shelters under the tree where a pigeon lives. He has the pigeon's mate in his cage. The pigeon is grieving her absence: where the beloved is, even the foot of a tree is home; without her, a palace is a wilderness (12.144.12).
what_they_did: The caged mate tells her husband to honour the man under their tree as a guest, enemy or not. The pigeon brings fire to warm the hunter and, having no food to give, throws himself into the fire so the guest may eat. The female, freed, follows him into the flames.
the_turn: The hunter breaks: 'This is the lesson given to me, the cruel one, by the great pigeon who burned his own flesh' (12.146.4). He throws away his nets and cage.
outcome: He gives up hunting, wanders in penance and later dies in a forest fire, his wrongs burned away. Bhishma tells this to teach that a refugee must be protected and that hospitality is owed even to an enemy: a tree does not withdraw its shade from the one who cuts it (12.145.5).
whole_arc_note: This story contains two self-sacrifices by fire, and the female's words idealise a wife following her husband in death. Do not present either as a model. The usable arc is the hunter's: a hard man undone by a kindness he did not deserve. Serve only where risk is none.
teaching: Kindness shown even to one's enemy can break a hard heart where nothing else could.
modern_parallels: I was cruel to my neighbour for years. When my house flooded, he was the first one to help. I could not look at him.
My father beat me and when he fell ill I still took care of him. Last week he cried and said sorry.
I said terrible things to a colleague and she covered for me the next day. I have not been the same since.
Some kindnesses feel like a slap. I did not deserve it and it changed me.

key_verses.gist: Where the beloved is, even the foot of a tree is home; without her a palace is a wilderness.
Hospitality is due even to an enemy; a tree does not withdraw its shade from the one who comes to cut it.

key_verses.sanskrit: नृशंसस्य ममाद्यायं प्रत्यादेशो न संशयः / दत्तः स्वमांसं दहता कपोतेन महात्मना
key_verses.gist: This is the lesson for me, the cruel one, from the pigeon who burned his own flesh.

content_hook: A hunter took shelter under the very tree where he had trapped a bird's mate.

title: The man who was rescued, fed and made rich, and killed his friend for the journey home
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Apaddharma Parva, Kritaghnopakhyana, adhyayas 166 to 172 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Gautama, a poor brahmin, is lost and starving. The crane Rajadharma takes him in as a guest, feeds him, and sends him to his friend the king Virupaksha, who loads him with gold. On the way home Gautama sleeps under the crane's tree, and the crane guards him through the night.
what_they_did: While the crane sleeps, Gautama thinks of the long road and his need for food, and kills him with a burning brand, happy, never thinking of the consequence (12.171.3). The king, missing his friend, sends his son, who finds the crane's body in the banyan (12.171.12).
the_turn: The verdict of the whole tale: there is atonement for the killer of a brahmin, the drunkard, the thief and the vow-breaker, but none for the ungrateful (12.172.17). Keep a grateful heart; a friend is the greatest blessing (12.172.20).
outcome: Gautama is executed and even the flesh-eaters will not touch his body. The crane is revived by grace and, asked what he wants, asks only that his killer be restored too.
whole_arc_note: The crane's last act, asking life for the man who killed him, is part of the story; do not stop at the punishment. The tale contains caste insults against Gautama for his way of life; leave those out when retelling.
teaching: Ingratitude to the one who helped you is the wrong for which the text sees no atonement.
modern_parallels: I gave my friend a job when no one else would. He took my clients and left.
My brother-in-law lived with us for two years. Now he tells people we used him.
I vouched for a colleague's promotion and he blocked mine.
The person I lent money to in his worst year now avoids my calls.

key_verses.sanskrit: ब्रह्मघ्ने च सुरापे च चोरे भ्रष्टव्रते तथा / निष्कृतिर्विहिता राजन्कृतघ्ने नास्ति निष्कृतिः
key_verses.gist: There is atonement for many wrongs, but none for the ungrateful.
Keep a grateful heart and a friendly spirit; a friend is the greatest blessing.

content_hook: The crane fed him, guarded him and made him rich. The man needed food for the road home.

title: Ordered by his father to kill his mother, the slow son thinks it over
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, Chirakari Upakhyana, adhyaya 272 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Chirakari is known for doing everything slowly; he thinks long, wakes long, sleeps long, and people call him lazy. One day his father, in a fit of anger at his wife, orders him: kill your mother, and leaves for the forest.
dilemma: How can I obey my father, and how can I not kill my mother? How do I not sink in this false dharma like a bad man (12.272.10)?
what_they_did: He does what he always does: he takes his time. He thinks through what a father is owed and what a mother is: there is no shade like a mother, no refuge like a mother, no one as dear as a mother (12.272.31). Who with any sense would kill the one who carried and nursed him?
the_turn: Meanwhile the father, his anger cooled, sees that his wife was wronged by another and that he himself was jealous: 'they say ruin is born of jealousy; it threw me into a sea of wrongdoing' (12.272.51). He hurries home praying: if only my son is slow today.
outcome: He finds his son has not acted. Overjoyed, he blesses him: Chirakari, bless you; if you are slow today, you are truly Chirakari (12.272.54). The text ends praising slow judgement: make friends slowly and part slowly; in anger, pride and harsh duties, the slow one is praised (12.272.69-73).
whole_arc_note: The mother was innocent; the father admits his own jealousy. Keep that, and never let the story read as if the mother's punishment were in question. The point is the son's refusal to act on an angry order, and the father's repentance.
teaching: When an order comes in anger, slowness is wisdom; think it through and you will not live with regret.
framework: Chirakari's rule: 1. When a command or impulse comes in heat, do not act on it today. 2. Weigh what each person is owed. 3. Give the angry one time to cool. 4. Decide slowly and you will not grieve long.
modern_parallels: My boss told me in a rage to fire someone on the spot. I waited until Monday and he thanked me.
My father ordered me to cut off my mother after their fight. I did not answer for a week.
I wrote a furious email to my brother and left it in drafts. I am glad I did.
My family calls me slow. This time it saved us.

key_verses.sanskrit: पितुराज्ञां कथं कुर्यां न हन्यां मातरं कथम् / कथं धर्मच्छले नास्मिन्निमज्जेयमसाधुवत्
key_verses.gist: How can I do my father's bidding, and how can I not kill my mother?
No shade like a mother, no refuge like a mother, no one as dear as a mother.
In every matter think it over and decide slowly; then you do not suffer regret for long.

content_hook: His father told him to kill his mother. Everyone called him slow. That saved her.

title: Asked how to live, the swan says: when they insult you, do not answer back
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, Hamsa Gita, adhyaya 305 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: The Sadhya gods see a golden swan wandering and ask it the question every one of us asks: what is the best way to live? The swan's whole answer turns on one daily ordeal: what to do when people speak harshly to you.
what_they_did: The swan says: arrows of words fly from the mouth, and the one they strike grieves day and night; a wise person does not send them at others (12.305.9). Insulted, I say nothing; struck, I forgive (12.305.12).
the_turn: 'Insulted, one should not insult back. The anger of one who bears it burns up the one who insulted him, and the patient one gains his merit' (12.305.16).
outcome: The Sadhyas take this as the highest teaching. Bhishma gives it to Yudhishthira as a rule of the free person.
whole_arc_note: The swan speaks of restraint in speech, not of accepting abuse or staying in danger. For someone being harmed, pair with stories that defend dignity; never use this to tell a wronged person to keep quiet about real wrong.
teaching: Do not return harsh words; the restraint of the one who bears them protects him and turns the harm back.
modern_parallels: My manager humiliated me in front of the team and I wanted to tear into him.
My mother-in-law says something cutting at every meal and I keep firing back.
Someone left a nasty comment on my post and I spent the night drafting replies.
My brother and I cannot have one conversation without trading insults.

key_verses.sanskrit: वाक्सायका वदनान्निष्यतन्ति / यैराहतः शोचति रात्र्यहानि / परस्य नामर्मसु ते पतन्ति / तान्पण्डितो नावसृजेत्परेषु
key_verses.gist: Arrows of words fly from the mouth, and the one struck grieves day and night; the wise do not shoot them.

key_verses.sanskrit: आक्रुश्यमानो नाक्रोशेन्मन्युरेवं तितिक्षतः / आक्रोष्टारं निर्दहति सुकृतं चास्य विन्दति
key_verses.gist: Insulted, do not insult back; the patience of the one insulted burns the insulter.

content_hook: The gods asked a swan how to live. It answered with what to do when someone insults you.

title: A king finds a sage lying content in the dust and asks how
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, Ajagara vow, adhyaya 177 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Prahlada, a wise king, meets a brahmin wandering without any work, untroubled and healthy, living like a python: eating what comes, lying where he is. Prahlada, who has everything, cannot understand how a man with nothing is so at ease, and asks him.
what_they_did: The sage answers gently: watch how creatures come into being, grow, decline and perish without our arranging it; I neither rejoice nor suffer at it (12.177.10). I do not refuse a rightful pleasure that comes on its own, nor do I chase one that is hard to get (12.177.24).
the_turn: His contentment comes from seeing what is not in his control and not straining against it, while still accepting what comes.
outcome: Prahlada honours him and goes. Bhishma tells it as the vow of the one who is content.
whole_arc_note: This is a portrait of contentment, not a command to stop working; Bhishma tells Yudhishthira many tales urging effort too. Use for people who are fine and want to stay fine, and for the restless, not for someone struggling to meet basic needs.
teaching: Accept what rightly comes, do not chase what is hard to get, and watch rise and fall without being thrown.
modern_parallels: My grandfather has nothing much and is the happiest person I know. I want to know his secret.
I have everything on my checklist and still feel like I am hunting for something.
I took a slower job and people think I gave up. I have never been calmer.
I am grateful for my small life and do not want to be told I should want more.

key_verses.gist: I do not refuse a rightful pleasure that comes on its own, nor chase one that is hard to get.

key_verses.sanskrit: पश्य प्रह्लाद भूतानामुत्पत्तिमनिमित्ततः / ह्रासं वृद्धिं विनाशं च न प्रहृष्ये न च व्यथे
key_verses.gist: Watch the rise, growth and end of beings without cause from us; I neither rejoice nor grieve.

content_hook: The king had everything. The man lying in the dust had nothing. Only one of them was at peace.

title: A woman ascetic tests the king who says he is free
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma Parva, Sulabha-Janaka Samvada, adhyaya 325 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: King Janaka is famous for saying he is liberated while still ruling. Sulabha, a wandering woman yogi, hears this and doubts it (12.325.9). She comes to his court to see for herself and, by yoga, enters his mind to test him.
what_they_did: Janaka, surprised and offended, demands to know who she is, whose she is, and lectures her on propriety and his own freedom, saying he is free even among royal parasols and thrones (12.325.20-22).
the_turn: Sulabha answers calmly, point by point: one who is truly free would not be disturbed by who she is or where she came from; his anger and his concern for status show the bonds he says he does not have. The self in her and in him is the same.
outcome: Janaka has no answer. The woman who came alone, with no rank, teaches the most celebrated philosopher-king of the age.
whole_arc_note: Sulabha is the teacher and the text gives her the last word. Keep her central. Janaka is not mocked; he is shown as someone whose words outran his practice.
teaching: Freedom is tested by how one reacts, not by what one says about oneself.
modern_parallels: I tell everyone I am detached from my job title. Then a junior questioned me in a meeting and I was furious.
I teach mindfulness and a student asked me why I was so rattled by one bad review.
My husband says he does not care what people think. A neighbour's remark ruined his week.
I say I am over my ex. Then I saw her photo and my whole day went.

key_verses.sanskrit: साऽतिसूक्ष्मां कथां श्रुत्वा तथ्यं नेति ससंशया / दर्शने जातसंकल्पा जनकस्य बभूव ह
key_verses.gist: Hearing the subtle claim, she doubted it was true, and resolved to see Janaka.

key_verses.sanskrit: छत्रादिषु विशेषेषु मुक्तं मां विद्धि तत्त्वतः / सत्वां संवेत्तुमिच्छामि मानार्हा हि मताऽसिमे
key_verses.gist: Janaka: know me to be truly free even amid the parasol and royal emblems.

content_hook: The king said he was spiritually free. A wandering woman came to check.

title: 'You were born after him. How could you have taught him?'
source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva; Bhagavad Gita 4.1-8
the_moment: Krishna says he taught this yoga long ago to the sun god Vivasvan, who passed it to Manu. Arjuna, who grew up with Krishna as cousin and friend, does the honest thing and objects: your birth is recent, his was ancient; how am I to understand that you taught it at the beginning?
what_they_did: He says his doubt out loud to his teacher instead of nodding along.
the_turn: Krishna does not rebuke the question. 'Many births of mine have passed, and of yours too, Arjuna; I know them all, you do not' (4.5). He goes on to say why he comes, age after age (4.7-8).
outcome: The doubt opens one of the Gita's central teachings. Honest objection is treated as part of learning.
whole_arc_note: Keep Krishna's answer with the question; the scene affirms asking, and the answer is a claim of divinity that the tradition (Shankara, Ramanuja) reads literally. Do not reduce it to 'question everything'.
teaching: An honest doubt, spoken to the teacher, opens the teaching instead of closing it.
modern_parallels: My guru said something that sounded impossible and I asked him how. Everyone looked at me.
I grew up with the stories and now I want real answers, not just 'have faith'.
I asked my grandmother how she can believe all this. She smiled and started telling me.
I am a scientist and I read the Gita with a pencil, writing 'how?' in the margins.

key_verses.sanskrit: अपरं भवतो जन्म परं जन्म विवस्वतः । कथमेतद्विजानीयां त्वमादौ प्रोक्तवानिति ॥
key_verses.gist: Your birth was later, Vivasvan's earlier; how am I to understand that you taught it first?

key_verses.sanskrit: बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन । तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परन्तप ॥
key_verses.gist: Many births of mine and yours have passed; I know them all, you do not.

content_hook: Arjuna interrupted God mid-sentence: 'That does not add up.'

title: An old mother, her son dead of snakebite, and the hunter who wants to kill the snake
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, opening adhyaya 1 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); Bhishma tells it to a guilt-stricken Yudhishthira
the_moment: Yudhishthira opens the book by saying he has no peace: looking at Bhishma's arrow-pierced body, he can think only of his own wrongs; this was done to you because of me (13.1.4-6). Bhishma answers with a story. Gautami, an old woman known for her calm, finds her son dead of a snakebite (13.1.18). A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it up and brings it to her: tell me how to kill it.
dilemma: Take revenge on the one who seems to have caused the death, or see the wider chain.
what_they_did: Gautami refuses, again and again, to let him kill it: killing it will not bring my boy back (13.1.24, 34). The snake pleads that Death drove it. Death arrives and says Time moved it. Time arrives and says: neither I, nor Death, nor the snake, nor this old woman is the cause; the child's own past action was (13.1.71, 77).
the_turn: Gautami herself concludes: neither Time, nor the snake, nor Death is the cause here; the boy met his end by his own karma in time; let the snake go (13.1.79-80). Then she and the hunter are both free of grief (13.1.81).
outcome: Bhishma turns it on Yudhishthira: this was not done by you, nor by Duryodhana; know that Time did it (13.1.83). Yudhishthira's fever lifts (13.1.84).
whole_arc_note: The story's two uses must stay apart. For the guilt-ridden survivor, its message is 'you were not the sole cause'. Its explanation for the child's death is the child's own past karma, which must never be told to a bereaved parent as consolation; do not serve this to a parent who has lost a child. Gautami's refusal of revenge is hers to make; do not use it to tell the wronged to let go.
teaching: A loss has many hands in it and none of them is the whole cause; seeing this frees both the griever and the one who blames himself.
modern_parallels: I keep thinking the war in our family was my doing. Everyone else says it had been coming for years.
My uncle died after the operation I pushed for, and I cannot stop blaming myself.
Everyone wants me to sue the driver. Suing will not bring her back, and I do not want my life to be that.
I was the manager on shift when it happened. I need to know it was not only me.

key_verses.sanskrit: शराचितं शरीरं हि तीव्रव्रणमुदीक्ष्य ते / शमं नोपलभे वीर दुष्कृतान्येव चिन्तयन्
key_verses.gist: Seeing your arrow-covered body and wounds, I find no peace, thinking only of my wrongs.

key_verses.sanskrit: नास्यामृतत्वं भवितैवं हतेऽस्मि- / ञ्जीवत्यस्मिन्कोऽत्ययः स्यादयं ते / अस्योत्सर्गे प्राणयुक्तस्य जन्तो- / र्मृत्युं लोके को न गच्छेदनन्ते
key_verses.gist: Killing it will not make him live; what harm if it lives? Who would escape death by killing one creature?

key_verses.sanskrit: नैव त्वया कृतं कर्म नापि दुर्योधनेन वै / कालेनैतत्कृतं विद्धि निहता येन पार्थिवाः
key_verses.gist: This was not done by you, nor by Duryodhana; know that Time did it.

content_hook: The hunter brought the snake to the grieving mother and asked how she wanted it killed.

title: The parrot who would not leave the dead tree
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, adhyaya 11 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: A hunter's poisoned arrow struck a great tree and it withered: leafless, fruitless, no shelter left. The parrot who had lived in its hollow all its life would not leave. It stayed on, not flying, not eating, weak and barely able to speak, grieving with the tree (13.11.7-8).
what_they_did: Indra comes in disguise and asks: why do you keep to a dry, fruitless tree that gives no shelter, when the whole forest is open to you (13.11.17)?
the_turn: 'I lived off it when it flourished; how can I leave it now that it is in trouble?' (13.11.26). Indra, moved by its loyalty and compassion, offers a boon.
outcome: The parrot asks only that the tree live again. Indra restores it with nectar, and the tree and the bird flourish together.
whole_arc_note: Bhishma tells this to praise compassion and loyalty to a dependant, not to say one must stay in any situation forever. The tree did no wrong to the parrot; do not use it for staying with someone who harms you.
teaching: Stay by the one who sheltered you when they flourished, now that they are failing.
modern_parallels: My father built this shop. It is failing now and everyone tells me to sell. He gave me everything when it was doing well.
My mother has dementia and my friends ask why I do not move her to a home. She raised four of us alone.
The startup that gave me my first break is going under. I am staying till the end.
My old teacher has no students left. I still go every Sunday.

key_verses.gist: I lived off it when it flourished; how can I leave it now that it is in trouble?

key_verses.sanskrit: निष्पत्रमफलं शुष्कमशरण्यं पतत्त्रिणाम् / किमर्थं सेवसे वृक्षं यदा महदिदं वनम्
key_verses.gist: Why do you keep to a leafless, fruitless, dry tree with no shelter, when the forest is so vast?

content_hook: The tree had died. Every bird had left. One parrot stayed, and refused to say why until a god asked.

title: A poor mother mixes flour in water and tells her boy it is milk
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Danadharma Parva, Upamanyu's account to Krishna, adhyaya 45, verses 96 onward (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Upamanyu, a sage's son growing up in a forest hermitage, sees a cow being milked and cries for milk: give me milk, mother (13.45.98-99). There is none. His mother, grieving at having nothing, mixes flour in water and gives it to him and his brother as milk (13.45.100-101). Then, at a relative's house, he tastes real milk, and comes home and says: this is not milk you gave me.
what_they_did: His mother, full of sorrow, holds him, kisses his head and tells him the truth: where would milk come from for forest-dwellers who live on roots and fruit (13.45.106-109)? Without the grace of Shiva, where would we get milk, comfort, clothes? Take refuge in him with all your heart (13.45.111-112).
the_turn: She does not pretend any longer and she does not shame the child for wanting. She gives him the truth and a refuge.
outcome: The boy goes on to do great austerity for Shiva, refuses every other offer in his trial, and is granted far more than milk. He tells this to Krishna as the root of his devotion.
whole_arc_note: The mother's grief and honesty are the scene; the devotional ending is the text's own and should not be dropped. Do not use to suggest poverty is solved by prayer alone; the text tells a lifetime of discipline after.
teaching: When you cannot give your child what they want, give them the truth and something greater to lean on.
modern_parallels: My son asked why we cannot go on holiday like his friends. I did not know whether to lie.
I told my kids the cheap brand was the same. My daughter tasted the real one at a party.
I have been pretending we are fine for months. My eldest has figured it out.
My child wants things I cannot afford and I feel like a failure every time I say no.

key_verses.sanskrit: ततः पिष्टं समालोड्य तोयेन सह माधव / आवयोः क्षीरमित्येव पानार्थं समुपानयत्
key_verses.gist: She mixed flour with water and brought it to us to drink, saying it was milk.

key_verses.sanskrit: ततो मामब्रवीन्माता दुःखशोकसमन्विता / पुत्रस्नेहात्परिष्वज्य मूर्ध्नि चाघ्राय माधव
key_verses.gist: Then my mother, full of grief, held me out of love and kissed my head.

key_verses.sanskrit: अप्रसाद्य विरूपाक्षं वरदं स्थाणुमव्ययम् / कुतः क्षीरोदनं वत्स सुखानि वसनानि च
key_verses.gist: Without the grace of Shiva, where would we get milk, comforts or clothes, child?

content_hook: She had no milk for her son, so she stirred flour into water. One day he tasted the real thing.

title: A king and queen serve a guest who seems determined to break them
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Danadharma Parva, Chyavana and Kushika, adhyayas 87 to 91 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: The sage Chyavana comes to King Kushika's palace and asks to be served. He sleeps for days and the king and queen must sit by him without rest. He orders a huge feast, then has it burned along with the bed and seat (13.88.21-22). He has them yoked to a chariot and drives them through the streets, striking them. Through all of it they show no anger (13.88.23).
what_they_did: They keep serving, without complaint and without a trace of resentment the sage can find.
the_turn: At the end Chyavana reveals that he was testing them, and that he found no fault. He says: do not be angry, good has come to you; and the king answers: I have no anger, we are purified by you (13.88.58-60). Chyavana shows them a palace of gold and blesses their line.
outcome: Their patience is rewarded in the story with a vision and a blessing for generations.
whole_arc_note: This is a test by a sage, announced at the end, with a reward. Real caregiving and real difficult elders give no such guarantee, and the text does not ask anyone to accept harm. Use for the inner work of serving a demanding person without bitterness, not to tell anyone to accept abuse.
teaching: Service without resentment, under provocation, is the strongest proof of a good heart.
modern_parallels: My father-in-law lives with us since his stroke and he finds fault with every meal.
My mother sends back the food, wakes me at 3 am, and then tells relatives I neglect her.
My boss gives impossible demands and then throws out the work. I have stopped getting angry and started watching what it does to me.
I care for my grandmother. Some days she is cruel. I want to serve her without becoming bitter.

key_verses.sanskrit: न च तौ चक्रतुः क्रोधं दम्पती सुमहाव्रतौ / तयोः सम्प्रेक्षतोरेव पुनरन्तर्हितोऽभवत्
key_verses.gist: That couple of great vows showed no anger at all.

key_verses.sanskrit: न मे मन्युर्महाभाग पूतौ स्वो भगवंस्त्वया / संवृतौ यौवनस्थौ स्वो वपुष्मन्तौ बलान्वितौ
key_verses.gist: I have no anger, lord; we have been purified by you.

content_hook: The guest burned the feast, then had the king and queen pull his chariot. They did not get angry once.

title: A worm runs from a cart, and Vyasa asks why it bothers to live
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, adhyayas 179 to 181 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about those who died in the war wanting or not wanting to die, and admits that giving up life is hard for anyone (13.179.2). Bhishma tells of Vyasa seeing a worm racing across a road. Asked why, the worm says: I heard a great cart coming and was afraid it would kill me; death is painful to creatures and life is hard to get, so I run (13.179.10-14).
what_they_did: Vyasa probes: what pleasure can a worm have? Death would be better for you (13.179.15-16). The worm answers: life clings everywhere; even here I have my pleasure; I am conscious, so I want to live (13.179.17). Then it remembers its last birth: a rich, cruel, envious man who fed no guest and gave no shelter (13.179.19-25), and it is ashamed.
the_turn: The worm recalls one good: it once honoured its old mother and a guest, and that is why its memory was not taken (13.179.27-28). It asks Vyasa what is truly good.
outcome: Vyasa promises to lift it, and over successive births it rises, until it reaches the highest goal.
whole_arc_note: Two truths sit together: every creature loves its life, and a selfish life is regretted. Do not use as 'you should be grateful you are not a worm'. The worm's past-birth caste and later rise through castes are in the text; tell it without endorsing hierarchy.
teaching: Every creature clings to life; what we will regret at the end is how we treated others.
modern_parallels: After my scan came back clear I realised how badly I want to live, even this ordinary life.
My grandfather in hospital says he does not want to die. People think that is weakness. I think it is honest.
I have been ruthless at work for twenty years and lately all I think about is the people I did not help.
I am afraid of dying and ashamed of being afraid.

key_verses.sanskrit: दुःखं हि मृत्युर्भूतानां जीवितं च सुदुर्लभम् / अतो भीतः पलायामि गच्छेयं नापदं यथा
key_verses.gist: Death is painful to beings and life is hard to come by; so I run in fear.

key_verses.sanskrit: सर्वत्र निरतो जीव इहापि च सुखं मम / चेतयामि महाप्राज्ञ तस्मादिच्छामि जीवितुम्
key_verses.gist: Life clings everywhere; even here I have my joy. I am conscious, so I want to live.

content_hook: Vyasa asked a worm why it was running for its life. The worm's answer made him stop.

title: A parent whose two families destroyed each other is offered one of them back
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, adhyaya 34 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: King Bhangashvana, who once held a sacrifice that left Indra out, is turned into a woman by Indra's anger after bathing in a lake. He gives the kingdom to his hundred sons and goes to the forest, where as a woman she has a hundred more sons with an ascetic. She brings them to the city to share the kingdom as brothers (13.34.25). By Indra's doing, enmity rises between the two sets, and they kill each other; she is left grieving two hundred sons (13.34.33, 38).
what_they_did: Indra reveals himself: I did this, for your sacrifice that slighted me. She falls at his feet and asks forgiveness (13.34.40-41). Pleased, Indra offers to revive one set of sons and asks which.
the_turn: She chooses the sons she bore as a woman, saying a mother's love is greater than a father's (13.34.44, 47). Pleased by her truthfulness, Indra revives them all (13.34.48).
outcome: Offered back manhood, she chooses to remain a woman. Bhishma tells the whole story to answer Yudhishthira's question about whether man or woman has greater pleasure in union, and the last part of the episode turns on that (13.34.1, 50-54).
whole_arc_note: Do not hide the frame: Bhishma tells this to answer a question about sexual pleasure, and the ending is about that. The usable core is the grief of a parent whose two families turned on each other, and the humility that won all of them back. Mark gender_sensitive. Do not use to make claims about women's nature.
teaching: A parent's love may favour one set of children, but humble truthfulness won back all of them.
modern_parallels: My children from my first marriage and my second will not speak to each other. I feel I made two families and lost both.
My sons fought over the property and now one will not attend the other's wedding.
I tried to make my stepchildren and my own kids one family and it blew up.
If I could save only one of my relationships with my children, I am ashamed of which one I would choose.

key_verses.sanskrit: पुरुषत्वे सुता यूयं स्त्रीत्वे चेमे शतं सुताः / एकत्र भुज्यतां राज्यं भ्रातृभावेन पुत्रकाः
key_verses.gist: You are my sons as a man, these hundred as a woman; enjoy the kingdom together as brothers.

key_verses.sanskrit: स्त्रियास्त्वभ्यधिकः स्नेहो न तता पुरुषस्य वै / तस्मात्ते शक्र जीवन्तु ये जाताः स्त्रीकृतस्य वै
key_verses.gist: A woman's love is greater than a man's; so let the sons I bore as a woman live.

content_hook: A king became a mother, raised two families, and watched them destroy each other.

title: After fifty-eight nights on the arrows, Bhishma asks leave to go
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Bhishma-svargarohana section, adhyaya 273 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: The bright half of Magha has come. Bhishma has been lying on sharp arrows, choosing his time. Yudhishthira arrives with the family. Bhishma says: fifty-eight nights have passed as I lay here, and on these sharpened arrows they have been like a hundred years (13.273.27-28).
what_they_did: He spends his last strength on the living. To Dhritarashtra, whose sons are all dead, he says: do not grieve; what was to be has been. Your sons were bent on anger and greed and overcome by envy; you should not mourn them (13.273.32, 35). Then he turns to Krishna and asks his leave: protect your devotee, calm, generous, owning nothing (13.273.39).
the_turn: He has kept his word to wait for the right time, and he lets go in devotion, not in exhaustion.
outcome: With Krishna's leave he withdraws his breath and departs. The family perform his last rites on the Ganga.
whole_arc_note: Bhishma's frankness to Dhritarashtra about his sons is part of it; do not soften it into general comfort. His long endurance was by choice and vow. Use for elders facing the end and for those sitting by them; not as a model of enduring pain without relief.
teaching: At the end, finish your duties to the living, speak plainly, and let go into what you trust.
modern_parallels: My grandfather waited until all of us had arrived from abroad, spoke to each of us, and went the next morning.
My father spent his last week settling every account and apologising to people. Then he asked for his mala.
I am 78 and I want to leave cleanly: debts paid, words said, nothing left hanging.
I sat with my mother in her last days. She was in pain and still kept asking about the grandchildren.

key_verses.sanskrit: अष्टपञ्चाशतं रात्र्यः शयानस्याद्य मे गताः / शरेषु निशिताग्नेषु यथा वर्षशतं तथा
key_verses.gist: Fifty-eight nights have passed as I lay on these sharp arrows; they have been like a hundred years.

key_verses.sanskrit: त्वद्भक्तं त्वद्गतिं शान्तमुदारमपरिग्रहम् / त्रायस्व पुण्डरीकाक्ष पुरुषोत्तम नित्यशः / अनुजानीहि मां कृष्ण वैकुण्ठ पुरुषोत्तम
key_verses.gist: Protect your devotee, calm, generous, owning nothing; give me leave, Krishna.

content_hook: Fifty-eight nights on a bed of arrows. Then Bhishma asked for permission to leave.

title: A mother outlives her very old son and asks why her heart does not break
source_ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Bhishma-svargarohana section, adhyaya 274 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Bhishma's water rites are done. The river goddess Ganga, his mother, rises from the water weeping and overwhelmed with grief (13.274.20). She recounts his greatness and says: my heart must be made of stone, for it does not break though I cannot see my beloved son (13.274.23).
what_they_did: She grieves openly in front of the family and asks why he, who could not be beaten, was killed by Shikhandi.
the_turn: Krishna and Vyasa console her: be at peace, he has gone to the highest world; he was one of the Vasus and has returned to them; do not grieve for him (13.274.28, 33).
outcome: She sets aside her grief and goes back into her waters (13.274.34).
whole_arc_note: Her guilt at not breaking is honest and common; keep it. The consolation is specific to Bhishma's divine origin; when used for a human parent, lean on her grief and the presence of those who sat with her, not on the promise.
teaching: Even a goddess grieves her child, however old; grief does not measure love, and comfort can come from those who stand with us.
modern_parallels: My son was 70 when he died. People think it is natural at that age. I am 93 and I buried my child.
I did not cry at the funeral and now I wonder what is wrong with me.
My mother keeps asking why she is still alive when her son is gone.
I feel guilty that I am still functioning after losing him.

key_verses.sanskrit: अश्मसारमयं नूनं हृदयं मम पार्थिवाः / अपश्यन्त्याः प्रियं पुत्रं यन्न दीर्यति मेऽद्य वै
key_verses.gist: My heart must be made of stone, for it does not break though I cannot see my son.

key_verses.sanskrit: तस्मान्मा त्वं सरिच्छ्रेष्ठे शोचस्य कुरुनन्दनम् / वसूनेष गतो देवि पुत्रस्ते विज्वरा भव
key_verses.gist: Do not grieve for him, best of rivers; your son has gone to the Vasus. Be free of fever.

content_hook: Bhishma was the oldest man on the battlefield. His mother still came out of the river to weep for him.

title: 'How does a steady person talk, sit and walk?'
source_ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Bhagavadgita Parva; Bhagavad Gita 2.54-72
the_moment: Krishna has just spoken of a mind that stands firm. Arjuna, still shaken, asks the most practical question in the book: what does such a person look like? How does he speak, how does he sit, how does he walk?
what_they_did: He asks for a picture of the goal in everyday terms rather than a theory.
the_turn: Krishna answers with a portrait: one who has let go of all the cravings of the mind and is content in the self (2.55); not shaken by sorrow, not craving pleasure, free of attachment, fear and anger (2.56); who draws in the senses like a tortoise its limbs (2.58).
outcome: The portrait becomes the most recited passage in the Gita, said daily in many ashrams.
whole_arc_note: Read as Arjuna's honest request, not a test answer; the tradition (Shankara) reads the marks both as the description of the realised and as the discipline of the seeker.
teaching: To grow steady, first see clearly what steadiness looks like in a person.
modern_parallels: I keep reading about calm. I want to know what a calm person actually does at 8 am on a Monday.
My grandmother never raised her voice in sixty years. I want to understand what was going on inside her.
Show me one person who is not anxious. I need a picture, not advice.
I want to know what I am aiming for before I start meditating.

key_verses.sanskrit: स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव । स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम् ॥
key_verses.gist: How is the steady one described? How does he speak, sit, walk?
One whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, who craves no pleasure, free from attachment, fear and anger, is steady.

content_hook: Arjuna's most practical question: what does a calm person actually look like?

title: Arjuna, after the war, admits he has forgotten what Krishna taught him
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, Anugita Parva, adhyaya 17 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI 14.16)
the_moment: The war is over and the kingdom won. Arjuna and Krishna are relaxing in the great hall. Arjuna says: I came to know your greatness when the battle stood before us. But all that you told me then out of friendship, I have lost, my mind was so scattered. I keep wanting to hear it again, and you will soon go back to Dvaraka (14.17.5-7).
what_they_did: He says it plainly to his teacher, without dressing it up.
the_turn: Krishna is displeased: I taught you the eternal truth, and you did not hold it, through your own lack of understanding; I cannot tell it again in the same way, for I spoke it then in yoga (14.17.9 onward). But he does not send him away. He teaches it again through an old story, the Anugita.
outcome: Arjuna receives the teaching a second time in a new form.
whole_arc_note: Keep Krishna's rebuke; it is part of the scene and the tradition reads it as a warning against careless listening. Keep also his second teaching; the door is not closed.
teaching: Even what changed your life can slip away in ordinary days; go back and ask again.
modern_parallels: I had a life-changing retreat three years ago. I cannot remember a single thing I learned.
In the ICU I promised myself I would live differently. Six months later I am exactly the same.
My guru told me something that saved me in my worst year. Now that life is good, I have forgotten it.
I read the Gita once in a crisis and want to read it again now that I am fine.

key_verses.sanskrit: यत्तु तद्भवता प्रोक्तं पुरा केशव सौहृदात् / तत्सर्वं पुरुषव्याघ्र नष्टं मे व्यग्रचेतसः
key_verses.gist: All that you told me before out of friendship, Keshava, I have lost, my mind was so distracted.

key_verses.sanskrit: श्रावितस्त्वं मया गुह्यं ज्ञापितश्च सनातनम् / धर्मं स्वरूपिणं पार्त सर्वलोकांश्च शाश्वतान्
key_verses.gist: I made you hear the secret, eternal teaching.

content_hook: After the war, Arjuna admitted something surprising: he had forgotten the Gita.

title: The king collapses on the riverbank, and Krishna tells him his real war has started
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, Ashvamedhika Parva, adhyayas 1 and 12 to 13 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Bhishma's last rites are over. Climbing out of the Ganga, his eyes full of tears, Yudhishthira falls on the bank like an elephant pierced by a hunter (14.1.3). He has the throne and cannot stop grieving. Weeks of counsel have not reached the bottom of it.
what_they_did: Krishna tells him: you remember none of the old humiliations, the exile, the forest, Draupadi kicked in Virata's court, and you will not remember them (14.12.10-12). The battle with Drona and Bhishma is over; now a battle has come that you must fight with your mind alone.
the_turn: 'A war is upon you where arrows are useless, and servants and kin too; you must fight it alone, with your own self' (14.12.15). And: 'mine' in two syllables is death; 'not mine' in three is the eternal (14.13.3).
outcome: Krishna's words, with the Kama Gita that follows, bring Yudhishthira to take up the horse sacrifice and his duty.
whole_arc_note: Krishna does not deny the grief; he names its new field. Keep the context: it is after victory that the inner war begins. Do not read 'not mine' as coldness; the tradition reads it as freedom from possessiveness. Bhima said the same words to him months earlier (12.16.21-22, see st.mbh.bhima_you_only_repeat_the_words); Krishna repeats them after the grief has run its course, and only now do they land.
teaching: After the outer battle is won, the war with one's own mind remains, and it is fought alone.
modern_parallels: I closed the funding round and collapsed in the car park.
We finally won custody and I cannot stop crying. The fight is over and the war in my head is not.
I got the promotion I fought for and I feel more lost than when I was struggling.
My father's case is settled. Now I have to deal with everything I felt during it.

key_verses.sanskrit: उत्तीर्य तु महाबाहुर्बाष्पव्याकुललोचनः / पपात तीरे गङ्गाया व्याधविद्ध इव द्विपः
key_verses.gist: Coming out of the water, eyes full of tears, he fell on the Ganga's bank like an elephant pierced by a hunter.

key_verses.sanskrit: यत्र नैव शरैः कार्यं न भृत्यैर्न च बन्धुभिः / आत्मनैकेन योद्धव्यं तत्ते युद्धमुपस्थितम्
key_verses.gist: A war where arrows, servants and kin are of no use; you must fight it alone, with yourself.

key_verses.sanskrit: द्व्यक्षरस्तु भवेन्मृत्युस्त्र्यक्षरं ब्रह्म शाश्वतम् / ममेति द्व्यक्षरो मृत्युर्नममेति च शाश्वतम्
key_verses.gist: 'Mine' is death; 'not mine' is the eternal.

content_hook: He won the war, buried his grandfather, and collapsed on the riverbank. Krishna said: now the real fight begins.

title: A sage, furious that God did not stop the war, threatens to curse him
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, Anugita Parva, the Uttanka (Udanka) episode, adhyayas 53 to 56 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Krishna, travelling home to Dvaraka after the war, meets his old friend the sage Uttanka in the desert. Uttanka asks after the Kurus and Pandavas. Hearing that the Kauravas are all dead, he flares up: you could have stopped it and you did not; I will curse you (14.53.19-21).
what_they_did: Krishna does not silence him. He says he tried everything for peace and they could not be brought to agree (14.53.15), and then explains who he is. At Uttanka's request he shows him the universal form; Uttanka bows and asks him to return to his own form (14.55.4-14).
the_turn: Krishna offers a boon; Uttanka asks for water whenever he needs it in the desert. When he is thirsty, an outcaste hunter with dogs appears and offers him water. Uttanka refuses again and again in disgust (14.55.25). The hunter vanishes. Krishna tells him: that was Indra bringing you amrita, and you turned it away.
outcome: Krishna grants that rain clouds will come to the desert when he thirsts (14.55.39). Uttanka has learned that his anger at God and his disgust at a person were the same blindness.
whole_arc_note: Keep both halves: the honest rage at God for allowing suffering, which Krishna hears and answers; and the test Uttanka fails through prejudice. Do not drop the second half, it is the teaching. Do not use the episode to endorse caste revulsion; it rebukes it.
teaching: Anger at God may be heard and answered; but grace can come in a form our prejudice refuses.
modern_parallels: My mother prayed every day of her life and died in pain. I am furious with God and I want an answer.
I asked how God could allow this war in my family. My guru did not tell me to stop asking.
Help came from the one person I had always looked down on, and at first I would not take it.
I told God I was done with him. Then the answer came from a stranger I would not have spoken to.

key_verses.sanskrit: न च ते प्रसभं यस्मात्ते निगृह्य निवारिताः / तस्मान्मन्युपरीतस्त्वां शप्स्यामि मधुसूदन
key_verses.gist: Since you did not restrain them by force, in anger I will curse you, Madhusudana.
I tried hard to bring the Kauravas to peace, but they would not agree.

key_verses.sanskrit: पुनःपुनश्च मातङ्ग पिबस्वेति तमब्रवीत् / न चापिबत्स सक्रोधः क्षुभितेनान्तरात्मना
key_verses.gist: 'Drink, drink,' the outcaste said again and again; angry and disturbed, he would not drink.

content_hook: A sage was so angry the war happened that he threatened to curse Krishna. Krishna let him speak.

title: A mongoose with half a golden body says the emperor's great sacrifice is worth less than a handful of flour
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, adhyayas 91 to 95, the mongoose's account at 92 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: At the end of Yudhishthira's magnificent horse sacrifice, a mongoose with one side of its body gold appears and says: this sacrifice does not equal a prastha of barley flour (14.92.93). Then it tells why. In a famine, a poor family who lived by gleaning grain had starved for days. At last they got a little barley flour and divided it into four. A hungry guest arrived.
what_they_did: The father gave the guest his share. The guest was still hungry. The wife gave hers, though hunger drives out sense and steadiness (14.92.69). Then the son gave his, then the daughter-in-law hers (14.92.27).
the_turn: The guest revealed himself as Dharma: by that handful of flour you have won the imperishable world (14.92.83). Rolling in the spilled flour and water where they had given, the mongoose found half its body turned to gold (14.92.88-89). It has rolled at every great sacrifice since, and none has turned the other half.
outcome: Yudhishthira's sacrifice, with all its gold, did not either. The text's line: one who has a thousand and gives a hundred, one who has a hundred and gives ten, and one who has nothing and gives a little water, are equal in merit (14.92.75).
whole_arc_note: Do not use this to shame people who give a lot, or to tell a poor family they must give what they cannot afford. The point is measure: what you give against what you have, given sincerely. The family's choice was free.
teaching: A small gift, honestly earned and given out of one's own need, outweighs a lavish one.
modern_parallels: Our housemaid sent money home for her neighbour's surgery. It was more than my whole year's donations, measured against what she has.
We gave a lot to the temple this year and I felt proud. Then I read this.
My mother fed every guest even when we had nothing. I used to be embarrassed. Now I understand.
I do not have much to give. I want to know if it still counts.

key_verses.sanskrit: सहस्रशक्तिश्च शतं शतशक्तिर्दशापि च / दद्यादपश्च यः शक्त्या सर्वे तुल्यफलाः स्मृताः
key_verses.gist: One with a thousand gives a hundred, one with a hundred gives ten, one with nothing gives water: equal in merit.

key_verses.sanskrit: विप्रस्य तपसा तस्य शिरो मे काञ्चनीकृतम् / तस्य सत्याभिसन्धस्य सक्तुदानेन चैव ह
key_verses.gist: By that sage's austerity and his gift of flour, my head became gold.
Hunger drives out wisdom and the sense of right.

content_hook: After the emperor's grandest ceremony, a half-golden mongoose walked in and said: not even close.

title: The heir is born still, and the grandmother tells Krishna to keep his promise
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, adhyayas 66 to 69 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Abhimanyu's widow Uttara gives birth, and the child, struck in the womb by Ashvatthama's weapon, is born dead. The women of the house, who have lost every son in the war, cry out: Vasudeva's sister's grandson is born dead (14.66.28). This was the one future left to them.
what_they_did: Kunti reminds Krishna of his vow at the Aishika: I will revive him (14.66.17-18). Subhadra falls at his feet: if you made this promise and do not keep it, count me dead too (14.67.9-13).
the_turn: Krishna swears by his own truth: I have never spoken a lie, even in jest; I have never turned back from battle; as truth and dharma are always established in me, may this child of Abhimanyu live (14.69.18-22).
outcome: The child breathes. He is named Parikshit, the one tested, and he will continue the line.
whole_arc_note: This is a miracle tied to Krishna's specific vow; it must never be served to a family who has lost a baby as consolation or hope. Its use is the women's grief and the power of truthfulness, and as a devotional story for those who are not newly bereaved.
teaching: Truth kept without exception carries power; the women's grief and Krishna's vow meet in one child.
modern_parallels: After everything our family lost, my nephew's birth felt like the one thing holding us together.
I made a promise to my sister in the hospital and I will move heaven and earth to keep it.
I have never lied to my children. Today that meant something.
I am a devotee and this is the story I read on the night my granddaughter was in the NICU and survived.

key_verses.sanskrit: त्वया ह्येतत्प्रतिज्ञातमैषीके यदुनन्दन / अहं संजीवयिष्यामि मृतं जातमिति प्रभो
key_verses.gist: At the Aishika you promised: I will revive the child born dead.

key_verses.sanskrit: नोक्तपूर्वं मया मिथ्या स्वैरेष्वपि कदाचन / न च युद्धात्परावृत्तस्तथा संजीवतामयम्
key_verses.gist: I have never spoken a lie, even in jest, nor turned back from battle; by that, let him live.

content_hook: Krishna's oath over a stillborn child: 'I have never told a lie, not even in jest.'

title: A son comes out humbly to greet his father, and is told to fight him
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, adhyayas 79 to 82 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
