the_moment: Arjuna arrives in Manipura following the sacrificial horse. His son Babhruvahana, whom he has barely known, comes out humbly to welcome him with brahmins at his side. Arjuna, angry, rejects the welcome: shame on you; a warrior who meets the man who came to fight him with soft words is no man (14.79.3-7). The boy stands with his head bowed.
dilemma: Honour his father by welcoming him, or honour his father by fighting him as he demands.
what_they_did: His stepmother Ulupi tells him to fight: that will please your father (14.79.11-12). He fights, and, young and strong, shoots his father through the heart; Arjuna falls, and Babhruvahana faints beside him (14.79.32-33).
the_turn: Chitrangada, seeing husband and son both fallen, laments (14.79.38). Ulupi revives Arjuna with a serpent gem and explains that this was the release of a curse Arjuna had earned by killing Bhishma unfairly.
outcome: Father and son are reconciled. Arjuna praises his son's valour.
whole_arc_note: Do not cut at the son's victory or at the father's insult. The text shows a father whose pride cost him; the son's courage is real and so is his anguish. Arjuna's taunt compares softness to a woman; leave that phrase out in retelling.
teaching: A child may have to stand up to a parent in the way the parent demands; the cost can be heavy and still lead to a truer bond.
modern_parallels: My father called me weak for being polite to him. When I finally pushed back, it went much further than I meant.
I tried to win my dad's approval by being agreeable. He only respected me when I argued.
My son and I competed for the same contract. He won. I am proud and hurt.
I barely knew my father. When he came back he wanted a fight, not a hug.

key_verses.sanskrit: धिक्त्वामस्तु सुदुर्बुद्धिं क्षत्रधर्माविशारदम् / यो मां युद्धाय सम्प्राप्तं साम्नैव प्रत्यगृह्णथाः
key_verses.gist: Shame on you, ignorant of a warrior's duty, who receive with peace one who came to fight.

key_verses.sanskrit: ततः स बाल्यात्पितरं विव्याध हृदि पत्रिणा / निशेतेन सुपुङ्खेन बलवद्बभ्रुवाहनः
key_verses.gist: Then the boy pierced his father in the heart with a sharp arrow.

content_hook: He came out to greet his father with folded hands. His father told him to pick up a bow.

title: After fifteen years as a guest in his nephew's palace, the old king asks to go
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, Ashramavasa Parva, opening adhyayas (Gita Press and BORI 15.1 to about 15.15; numbers from memory)
the_moment: For fifteen years Yudhishthira has treated his blind uncle as king, with every honour. But Bhima, within his hearing, keeps reminding him whose sons are dead and whose arms did it. Dhritarashtra has quietly begun eating once a day and lying on the floor. One day he tells Yudhishthira: I want to go to the forest. I am old, my sons are gone, let me do what the old should do.
dilemma: Stay comfortable and dependent in the house of the people his sons wronged, or leave everything for the forest at his age.
what_they_did: Yudhishthira is shattered: I did not know you were suffering; let me go to the forest and you rule. Dhritarashtra faints from weakness. Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to let him go; it is his time. The old king then stands before the citizens and asks their forgiveness for his son's rule and his own failures.
the_turn: He chooses to go while he can still choose, with Gandhari, asking pardon of the people rather than defending himself.
outcome: He leaves for the forest, with Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Sanjaya, and lives in austerity by the Ganga.
whole_arc_note: Keep both sides: Yudhishthira's sincere care and Bhima's quiet cruelty. The old man's leaving is his own choice, guided by Vyasa, not an exile. Do not read it as 'elders should get out of the way'.
teaching: When the time comes, an elder may choose to lay down his place with dignity and ask forgiveness for what he could not set right.
modern_parallels: My father lives with us since Mum died. He says he feels like a burden, though we never say it. One of us sometimes does.
My mother wants to move to an ashram at 74. We feel we have failed her.
I am 70 and I live in my son's house. I want to leave before I become a weight.
My father-in-law apologised to the whole family at his 80th birthday. No one knew what to say.

key_verses.ref: Ashramavasika Parva, Ashramavasa Parva (adhyaya not verified)
key_verses.gist: Dhritarashtra asks the citizens to forgive him and his son, and to look on Yudhishthira kindly.

content_hook: For fifteen years the blind king lived in the palace of the men who killed his sons. Then he asked to leave.

title: Her sons beg her to stay in the palace she fought for, and Kunti walks to the forest
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, Ashramavasa Parva (Gita Press about adhyayas 16 to 17; BORI about 15.22 to 15.23; numbers from memory)
the_moment: As Dhritarashtra and Gandhari set out, Kunti goes with them, guiding Gandhari's hand. Yudhishthira and Bhima follow her, weeping: you urged us to war through Vidula's story, you sent Krishna with words to rouse us; now that the kingdom is won, why are you leaving us?
dilemma: Stay and enjoy the kingdom with her sons, or go and serve the old couple and her own soul.
what_they_did: She does not turn back. She tells them: I roused you so you would not live in humiliation and so that dharma would be restored, not so that I could enjoy a throne. I had enough of royal life with your father. Now I want to serve my elders and do austerity.
the_turn: Her fight was for her sons' dignity, not for her own comfort, and she proves it by leaving at the moment of victory.
outcome: The sons turn back in tears. Kunti spends her last years serving Gandhari and Dhritarashtra.
whole_arc_note: Do not read this as a mother abandoning her children; she has finished her work and chooses her own path. Keep her stated reason.
teaching: One who fought for others' dignity does not need to collect a reward; she can walk away when the work is done.
modern_parallels: My mother pushed us so hard through school. Now that we are settled she has moved to Rishikesh and will not come back.
I fought for my children's rights in the divorce for years. Now they are grown and I want my own life.
My kids keep asking why I will not move in with them. I did not raise them to be cared for by them.
I spent my life building the family business for my sons. I am handing it over and leaving the city.

key_verses.ref: Ashramavasika Parva, Ashramavasa Parva (adhyaya not verified)
key_verses.gist: Kunti: I spurred you on so that you would not live as the defeated, not to enjoy the kingdom myself.

content_hook: She sent her sons to war to win back a kingdom. The day they won, she left.

title: Yudhishthira finds Vidura in the forest, and Vidura gives himself to him
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, Ashramavasa Parva (Gita Press about adhyaya 26; BORI about 15.33; numbers from memory)
the_moment: The Pandavas visit the elders in the forest. Vidura is not there; he wanders alone, naked, wasted by austerity, living on air. Yudhishthira runs after him through the forest calling: I am Yudhishthira, your dear one. Vidura stops in a lonely place and leans against a tree.
what_they_did: Vidura fixes his gaze on Yudhishthira, eyes to eyes, and by yoga enters his body, breath to breath, limb to limb. His own body stays standing against the tree, empty.
the_turn: Yudhishthira feels himself filled with his uncle's strength. A voice tells him not to cremate the body: Vidura was a renunciate and Dharma itself.
outcome: Yudhishthira returns to the elders and tells them. Vyasa reveals that Vidura and Yudhishthira were both born of Dharma.
whole_arc_note: This is a death, told as a giving. Keep the strangeness; do not convert it to metaphor only. For the bereaved it says the one who taught you lives on in you, which the text states literally.
teaching: The one who taught us can pass into us; what he was continues in the one he chose.
modern_parallels: My grandfather went quiet in his last months. The last thing he did was look at me for a long time.
Since my mentor died, I hear his voice when I make decisions.
I chased my uncle for years to reconcile. He finally looked at me, and he was gone a week later.
My mother's way of speaking comes out of my mouth now.

key_verses.ref: Ashramavasika Parva, Ashramavasa Parva (adhyaya not verified)
key_verses.gist: Vidura, by yoga, entered Yudhishthira's body: gaze into gaze, breath into breath.

content_hook: Yudhishthira chased his uncle through the forest. When he caught up, Vidura leaned against a tree and looked at him.

title: For one night, the dead rise out of the Ganga to meet the living
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, Putradarshana Parva (BORI about 15.36 to 15.44; numbers from memory)
the_moment: Fifteen years after the war, the old people in the forest still grieve. Gandhari asks Vyasa: Dhritarashtra cannot sleep for his sons, Kunti longs to see Karna, Draupadi her sons. Can we see them once?
what_they_did: Vyasa takes them to the Ganga at night and calls the dead out of the water: Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Abhimanyu, Draupadi's sons, Duryodhana and his brothers, all as they were in life but free of anger and envy. Dhritarashtra is given sight for that night. Families embrace; Kunti meets Karna; enemies meet without hatred.
the_turn: The dead show no grudge. Meeting them whole and at peace dissolves much of the grief the living were carrying.
outcome: At dawn the dead return to the river. Vyasa tells the widows that those who wish may join their husbands, and some enter the water. The living go back lighter.
whole_arc_note: The scene's ending includes widows choosing to follow their husbands into the river; this must not be presented as a model, and the episode should be told with that part named, not hidden. Do not offer the night as something the bereaved can expect; offer the image of the dead at peace and without anger.
teaching: Those we lost, and those we fought, are at peace beyond anger; seeing that can loosen what we carry.
modern_parallels: I dreamed of my father and he was not angry with me. I woke up and cried for an hour.
I never made peace with my brother before he died. I want to believe he holds nothing against me.
Fifteen years later I still cannot sleep for my son.
I would give anything for one night with my mother.

key_verses.ref: Ashramavasika Parva, Putradarshana Parva (adhyaya not verified)
key_verses.gist: The dead rose from the Ganga free of anger and envy, and met the living.

content_hook: Fifteen years after the war, Vyasa called the dead out of the river for one night.

title: News comes that his mother died in a forest fire, far from him
source_ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, Naradagamana Parva (BORI about 15.45 to 15.47; numbers from memory)
the_moment: Two years later Narada comes to Hastinapura with news. Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti, frail and living on almost nothing, were caught by a forest fire. Sanjaya urged them to flee. They sat down facing east in meditation and let the fire take them. Sanjaya escaped to the Himalayas.
what_they_did: Yudhishthira breaks down: our mother, who had sons like us, burned to death like someone with no one. What use is our strength, our kingship? He cannot bear that she died alone while they lived in comfort.
the_turn: Narada tells him the fire that took them was the elders' own sacred fire, left burning in the forest, and that they went by their own choice, seated in yoga, to the highest end. They chose their going.
outcome: The Pandavas perform their rites. Yudhishthira's grief continues for a time, but the knowledge that it was their choice and their peace softens it.
whole_arc_note: The elders' choice to stay in the fire is presented by the text as a yogic end, not as despair; do not model it. The usable part is the son's guilt at a parent dying far away, and the reframe that the parent chose their way.
teaching: A parent who chose their own path and end was not abandoned; the child's guilt can rest on that truth.
modern_parallels: My mother died in the village while I was in Bangalore. I keep thinking she died alone.
Dad insisted on staying in his own house. He fell and we found him the next morning.
I was abroad when my grandmother passed. Everyone says she was at peace. I want to believe it.
My parents refused to move in with us. Now one of them is gone and I feel I should have forced them.

key_verses.ref: Ashramavasika Parva, Naradagamana Parva (adhyaya not verified)
key_verses.gist: Yudhishthira: she who had sons like us burned like one who had no one.

content_hook: His mother died in a forest fire, far from her five powerful sons. Narada told him what had really happened.

title: Bored young men play a joke on visiting sages, and a whole clan begins to end
source_ref: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, adhyayas 1 to 2 (Gita Press and BORI; numbers from memory)
the_moment: Thirty-six years after the war, the Yadavas of Dvaraka are rich, safe and careless. Some young men dress Krishna's son Samba as a pregnant woman and ask three visiting sages, mockingly, what she will give birth to. The sages see through it and say: he will bear an iron pestle that will destroy your clan.
what_they_did: Samba produces the pestle. The king has it ground to powder and thrown into the sea, bans liquor in the city, and everyone carries on. The powder washes up and grows as tall reeds on the shore. Krishna, who sees Gandhari's curse ripening, does not try to stop it.
the_turn: The text marks the turn in the joke itself: prosperity had made them contemptuous of those they should honour, and that contempt is where the ruin starts.
outcome: The omens multiply in Dvaraka. The ending is already in motion.
whole_arc_note: Read with the next episode; this is the cause, not the whole story. The pregnancy joke is the text's detail; tell it without making a woman the butt of the joke.
teaching: Prosperity that makes us careless and contemptuous plants the seed of its own end.
modern_parallels: Our company had ten easy years and the young team started mocking the old clients. We lost them all in one quarter.
My son has never known struggle and laughs at elders' advice. It frightens me.
We thought grinding the problem to dust and hiding it would make it go away. It grew back.
Our family got rich fast and stopped respecting anyone. I can see where it is heading.

key_verses.gist: The sages: he will bear an iron pestle that will destroy the Vrishnis and Andhakas.

content_hook: It began with a prank. A few bored young men dressed a boy up and mocked three sages.

title: On a drunken holiday, an old wound is reopened and a clan kills itself
source_ref: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, adhyaya 3 (Gita Press and BORI; numbers from memory)
the_moment: The Yadavas go to Prabhasa on the coast for a festival and drink heavily. Satyaki, drunk, sneers at Kritavarma for the night massacre of the sleeping Pandava camp years before. Kritavarma sneers back about Satyaki killing Bhurishravas when his arm was cut off. Old wounds from a war long over are torn open in front of everyone.
what_they_did: Satyaki leaps up and cuts off Kritavarma's head. The others fall on Satyaki; Pradyumna defends him and both are killed. Then everyone seizes the reeds growing on the shore, which in their hands become iron clubs, and fathers kill sons, sons fathers, until almost no one is left.
the_turn: Krishna watches and lets it happen; in the end he strikes down those who remain. The curse and the clan's own arrogance and drink have done what no enemy could.
outcome: The Vrishnis and Andhakas are destroyed. Krishna and Balarama prepare to leave the world.
whole_arc_note: This is the darkest episode in the epic's ending; keep it whole and do not make it entertainment. Its lesson is about unhealed grudges, alcohol and contempt, not about violence as spectacle.
teaching: Grudges never laid to rest, stirred by drink and pride, can destroy a family no enemy could touch.
modern_parallels: Every family wedding, after a few drinks, someone brings up the property dispute from 1998.
My uncles stopped speaking at my cousin's engagement because someone mentioned an old insult.
Our cofounders were fine for years until one offsite with too much alcohol.
My father and his brother still argue about who betrayed whom thirty years ago.

key_verses.gist: The eraka reeds became iron clubs in their hands, and kin killed kin.

content_hook: Thirty-six years after the war, two old soldiers got drunk and brought up what each had done that night.

title: A hunter shoots at a deer, and finds he has hit Krishna
source_ref: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, adhyaya 4 (Gita Press; BORI about 16.5; numbers from memory)
the_moment: After the clan is gone and Balarama has left his body, Krishna lies alone in the forest, deep in yoga. A hunter named Jara, mistaking his foot for a deer, shoots an arrow into it. He runs up and finds he has wounded the Lord. He falls at Krishna's feet in horror.
what_they_did: Krishna comforts the terrified hunter and reassures him. Then, his work in the world done, he departs, filling the sky with light.
the_turn: The one who was wronged consoles the one who did the wrong. Krishna, who knew this end was coming, does not let the hunter carry it as a crime.
outcome: Krishna returns to his own abode. Daruka has already been sent to bring Arjuna.
whole_arc_note: The death of Krishna is told quietly in the text; keep it quiet. The hunter's guilt and Krishna's comfort are the human centre. Do not turn it into a message that accidental harm does not matter; the hunter's horror is right, and the comfort is grace.
teaching: Even at his death Krishna comforts the one who wounded him by mistake.
modern_parallels: I was driving when the accident happened. My friend in the passenger seat, dying, told me it was not my fault.
I gave my father the wrong dose. He held my hand and said, do not carry this.
I made a mistake at work that cost someone their job, and they were the one who comforted me.
I hurt someone I love without meaning to and they forgave me before I could ask.

key_verses.gist: Jara, seeing whom he had struck, fell at his feet; Krishna comforted him.

content_hook: The hunter thought he was shooting a deer. When he got closer, he saw it was Krishna.

title: The greatest archer cannot string his bow, and Vyasa tells him why
source_ref: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, adhyayas 7 to 8 (Gita Press; BORI about 16.8 to 16.9; numbers from memory)
the_moment: Arjuna arrives at an empty Dvaraka, sees Vasudeva die of grief, and sets out to take the surviving women, children and elders to safety. On the road a band of cowherd robbers attacks. Arjuna, who once held off the whole world, can barely string the Gandiva. He cannot remember his divine weapons. His inexhaustible quivers run out. The robbers carry off many of those he was protecting while he stands there.
what_they_did: He brings the rest to Kurukshetra, settles Krishna's great-grandson Vajra on a throne, and then goes to Vyasa's hermitage, pale and hollowed, and tells him everything: Krishna is gone, my strength is gone, I could not protect them.
the_turn: Vyasa tells him: all of this has its root in Time. Your weapons and strength served their purpose while their time lasted; that time is over. Those same robbers were the instruments of a curse. It is now time for you to go too.
outcome: Arjuna returns to Yudhishthira with Vyasa's words, and the brothers decide to leave the world.
whole_arc_note: Do not soften the failure; the text lets Arjuna be powerless. Vyasa's answer is not 'you did your best' but 'your season is over', which is both hard and freeing. The abduction of women is a fact in the story; tell it as Arjuna's failure to protect, not as a spectacle.
teaching: Strength and skill are given for a season; when the season ends, know it, and let go.
modern_parallels: I was the best surgeon in the hospital for twenty years. Last month my hands shook in theatre.
I could always protect my family. When the floods came I could do nothing.
My mentor died and all my confidence went with him.
I am 62 and the skills that made my name do not work in this market any more.

key_verses.gist: Vyasa to Arjuna: all this has its root in Time; your weapons have done their work, and now it is time to go.

content_hook: Arjuna, the greatest archer in the world, could not string his bow. Vyasa told him why.

title: On the last walk, one by one they fall, and Bhima asks why
source_ref: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva, adhyayas 1 to 2 (Gita Press and BORI; from memory)
the_moment: The five brothers and Draupadi crown Parikshit, put on bark garments and set out on foot, walking north toward Meru, a dog following them. Arjuna throws the Gandiva into the sea when Agni asks. On the mountain, Draupadi falls. Bhima calls out: she never did wrong; why did she fall?
what_they_did: Yudhishthira answers without stopping: she was partial to Arjuna. Then Sahadeva falls: he thought no one was as wise as he. Nakula: he thought no one was as handsome. Arjuna: he boasted he would destroy all enemies in a day and looked down on other archers. At last Bhima himself falls and asks why; he ate too much and boasted of his strength.
the_turn: Yudhishthira does not look back. Each fall is named by the one small flaw that person carried to the end.
outcome: Yudhishthira walks on alone, with the dog.
whole_arc_note: Do not read Yudhishthira as cold; he has made his grief already and the walk is a renunciation. Draupadi's 'fault' is the text's reading; present it as Yudhishthira's verdict, not as a statement about women. This is a story about the small vanities that stay with us to the end.
teaching: Each person carries some small pride to the very end; the last journey reveals it.
modern_parallels: At my father's last days the one thing he could not let go of was being right.
I retired and realised my real attachment was to being admired, not to the job.
My grandmother, at 90, still could not stop comparing her children.
I want to know which small vanity I will still be carrying at the end.

key_verses.gist: Yudhishthira names the fault of each one who falls, and walks on without looking back.

content_hook: They walked toward the mountain together. One by one, they fell. Bhima kept asking why.

title: Offered heaven if he leaves the dog behind, Yudhishthira refuses
source_ref: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva, adhyaya 3 (Gita Press and BORI 17.3; from memory)
the_moment: Alone now except for the dog that has followed him the whole way, Yudhishthira is met by Indra in his chariot, come to take him to heaven in his body. Yudhishthira asks for his brothers and Draupadi, and is told they are already there. As he steps up, Indra says: the dog cannot come. Leave it.
dilemma: Heaven itself, after a lifetime of loss, or a stray dog that trusted him.
what_they_did: He refuses. Abandoning one who is devoted to you, who has come to you for shelter, is as great a wrong as killing a brahmin, he says. I will not give up this dog to gain heaven. Indra presses him again; he does not move.
the_turn: The dog changes form and stands as Dharma, his own father, who says: this was a test, and you have passed it, as you passed the test at the lake.
outcome: Yudhishthira rises to heaven in his body. Even there, the tests are not over.
whole_arc_note: The text gives the reason in Yudhishthira's own words: loyalty to one who depends on you. Keep that reason. Do not end at 'he got into heaven'; the next episode tests him again.
teaching: Do not abandon one who is devoted to you, not even for heaven.
modern_parallels: The new job came with a flat that does not allow pets. I said no to the job.
My company offered me a partnership if I let my oldest team member go. I could not.
Everyone said put Dad in a home and take the posting abroad. I did not go.
My dog stayed by me through the worst year of my life. I am not leaving him for anything.

key_verses.gist: I will not abandon one devoted to me, even for heaven.

content_hook: Indra opened the door to heaven and said: the dog stays here.

title: Yudhishthira reaches heaven and finds Duryodhana seated there in glory
source_ref: Mahabharata, Svargarohana Parva, adhyaya 1 (Gita Press and BORI; from memory)
the_moment: Yudhishthira enters heaven expecting his brothers. Instead he sees Duryodhana, radiant, seated on a throne and honoured by the gods. He turns away in anger: I do not want to share a world with the man who dragged Draupadi into the hall and caused the death of everyone we loved. Where are my brothers?
what_they_did: Narada smiles and tells him: do not say this. In heaven enmity ends. Duryodhana fought by the warrior's code and fell facing the enemy; give up your hostility here.
the_turn: Yudhishthira will not accept a heaven without his brothers and Karna. He says: wherever they are is heaven for me.
outcome: He is taken to find them, and the path leads into darkness.
whole_arc_note: Do not resolve this by saying Duryodhana was good. The text keeps his wrongs and still says the grudge must end. Yudhishthira's anger is real and named. Pair with the next episode.
teaching: Even the righteous must put down the grudge before they can rest; enmity has no place in heaven.
modern_parallels: The colleague who sabotaged me got a lifetime award. I could not sit through the ceremony.
My abusive uncle was praised at his funeral as a pillar of the community.
My ex is happy and successful and I am still angry.
I did everything right and the person who cheated is doing better than me.

key_verses.gist: Narada: in heaven there is no enmity; give up your hostility to Duryodhana.

content_hook: He reached heaven and the first person he saw was the man who had destroyed his family.

title: In the darkness, voices beg him to stay, and Yudhishthira chooses hell
source_ref: Mahabharata, Svargarohana Parva, adhyayas 2 to 3 (Gita Press and BORI; from memory)
the_moment: Led down a path of stench, blood and darkness, Yudhishthira cannot bear it and turns to go back. Voices call from all sides: stay a moment; while you are here a cool breeze blows and our pain eases. He asks who they are. They answer: Karna, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, Draupadi, Draupadi's sons.
what_they_did: Anger rises in him against the gods and against Dharma itself: what sin did they commit, and what good did Duryodhana do? Then he decides: go back and tell your masters I am staying here. My presence comforts my brothers; I will not leave them.
the_turn: Indra and Dharma appear and the illusion vanishes. This, they say, was the last test, and also the price of the half-truth he told Drona: a short sight of hell for a deception. Every king must see hell once.
outcome: He bathes in the heavenly Ganga, gives up his human body and with it his anger and grief, and joins his family in their divine forms.
whole_arc_note: Keep the anger at the gods; the text allows it. Keep the reason: the half-truth to Drona. And keep the choice: he chose to stay in pain to comfort others before he knew it was a test.
teaching: To stay with those you love in their pain, choosing it freely, is the last and highest test of dharma.
modern_parallels: My brother is in prison and everyone says to cut him off. When I visit, he calms down. I am not stopping.
My mother's ward is a terrible place. I stay because she sleeps when I am there.
I could have taken the transfer and left the team in the mess. I stayed.
I am angry at God for what happened to my family. I am also not leaving them.

key_verses.gist: Go back to those you serve; I will stay here, where my presence eases my brothers.

content_hook: The voices in the dark said: stay a little longer, it hurts less when you are here. Yudhishthira stayed.

title: Draupadi tells her husband: you promised us, and now you are breaking our hearts
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 14 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ); one of the family speeches, see also st.mbh.family_argues_yudhishthira_back
the_moment: Her four brothers-in-law have each argued with Yudhishthira and he has answered none of them; he sits silent, set on leaving for the forest. Draupadi, who has lost all five of her sons in this war, speaks to him gently and then plainly. Your brothers are drying up like thirsty chataka birds, calling to you, and you do not even cheer them (12.14.6).
what_they_did: She reminds him of what he himself said in the Dvaita forest, when they were cold, wind-beaten and humiliated: we will defeat Duryodhana, rule the earth and perform great sacrifices, and the forest's misery will turn to joy. You said that, she says; how can you crush our hearts now (12.14.8-12)?
the_turn: She does not argue philosophy; she holds him to his word and to the people who suffered alongside him, and tells him a ruler's duty is to protect and to punish, not to run.
outcome: Yudhishthira still does not yield at once; it takes Arjuna, Bhima, Vyasa and Krishna as well. Her speech is one of the voices that slowly bring him back.
whole_arc_note: Draupadi speaks as a bereaved mother who still chooses to call him back to duty; keep her grief in view. One line in her speech uses an insult about manhood; leave it out in retelling. Her argument is about keeping one's word to those who suffered with you.
teaching: You do not get to walk away from the people who endured everything on the strength of your promise.
modern_parallels: My husband sold the company we built together and now wants to go live in an ashram. I carried this family through the hard years on his promise.
We sacrificed everything for his MBA and now he says none of it matters.
My father led us through bankruptcy and now that we are back on our feet he says he wants to disappear.
I need my partner to remember what he told me on the worst night of our lives.

key_verses.sanskrit: इमे ते भ्रातरः पार्थ शुष्यन्ते स्तोकका इव / वावाश्यमानास्तिष्ठन्ति न चैनानभिनन्दसे
key_verses.gist: Your brothers are drying up like thirsty chataka birds, calling, and you do not cheer them.

key_verses.sanskrit: इत्येतानेवमुक्त्वा त्वं स्वयं धर्मभृतां वर / कथमद्य पुनर्वीर विनिहंसि मनांसि नः
key_verses.gist: Having said all that to them yourself, how can you now crush our hearts?

content_hook: She had lost all five of her sons. She still stood up and told her husband: you promised us.

title: Bhima tells his brother: you know the books and miss their meaning
source_ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva, adhyaya 10 and adhyaya 16 (Kumbakonam-edition numbering as in the local corpus; BORI and Gita Press numbers differ)
the_moment: Yudhishthira keeps answering grief with scripture: renunciation is the highest path, the forest is better than a throne won with blood. Bhima, who is no philosopher and knows it, loses patience. Your understanding, he says, is like a dull reciter's who knows the words by rote; it has been struck by repetition and does not see the real meaning (12.10.1).
what_they_did: He speaks bluntly, as only a brother can: if you meant to renounce, why did we fight and kill? Later he speaks again, holding his temper: I had decided not to say anything, but out of great pain I will speak (12.16.3). He tells him the battle with Drona and Bhishma is over and a new one has come, to be fought with the mind alone, where arrows, friends and kin are no use (12.16.21-22).
the_turn: The bluntest brother names what the others circle around: Yudhishthira is using spiritual language to avoid the duty in front of him.
outcome: Yudhishthira does not yield to Bhima alone, but the charge stays with him and is answered later by Vyasa and Krishna.
whole_arc_note: Bhima is harsh, and the text lets him be. Do not present his words as cruelty; they come from love and pain, and he says so. Use for people whose spirituality has become a way out of responsibility, and for the frank sibling who has to say so.
teaching: Words of scripture repeated without their meaning can become a hiding place from duty.
modern_parallels: My brother quotes the Gita every time we ask him to help with Dad's care.
I hide behind 'detachment' whenever my wife asks me to make a hard decision.
My sister finally told me I talk like a guru and act like a teenager.
I have read all the books and I still cannot face my own life.

key_verses.sanskrit: श्रोत्रियस्येव ते राजन्मन्दकस्याविपश्चितः / अनुवाकहता बुद्धिर्नैषा तत्त्वार्थदर्शिनी
key_verses.gist: Your mind, like a dull reciter's, is struck by rote repetition and does not see the real meaning.

key_verses.sanskrit: न वक्ष्यामि न वक्ष्यामीत्येवं मे मनसि स्थितम् / अतिदुःखात्तु वक्ष्यामि तन्निबोध जनाधिप
key_verses.gist: I had resolved not to speak, but out of great pain I will speak.

key_verses.sanskrit: यत्र नास्ति शरैः कार्यं न मित्रैर्न च बन्धुभिः / आत्मनैकेन योद्धव्यं तत्ते युद्धमुपस्थितम्
key_verses.gist: A war where arrows, friends and kin are of no use; you must fight it alone, with your own self.

content_hook: Bhima finally said what no one else would: you know every scripture, and you are using them to run away.
